name: Gossip Protocol
intent: Spread information through a cluster by having every node regularly tell a few random peers, so news reaches everyone quickly without any central coordinator.
scenario: A cluster of 1,000 database nodes must all learn that node 412 has died, or that a new node has joined. Sending the news from one place would overload it and fail if that place fails.
problem: Every node in a large cluster needs a roughly current view of membership, health and configuration. A central server is a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Broadcasting to everyone from everyone costs a quadratic number of messages. Yet the cluster must keep working when many nodes fail and links are unreliable.

howItWorks.title: Periodically pick a few random peers
howItWorks.text: Every second or so, each node picks a small number of other nodes at random (the fanout, often 1 to 3) and exchanges what it knows with them. There is no central schedule and no fixed topology, and every node does the same amount of work.

howItWorks.title: Information spreads like an epidemic
howItWorks.text: A node that learns something tells a few others. Each of them tells a few more on their next round. The number of informed nodes roughly doubles each round, so the whole cluster is informed in about log N rounds: around 10 rounds for 1,000 nodes, and still only about 20 for a million.

howItWorks.title: Exchange state, not only events
howItWorks.text: Nodes usually swap summaries (a version number or timestamp per entry) and send whatever the other side is missing, so the exchange fixes differences in both directions. This also repairs anything missed because a message was lost, since the next round tries again.

howItWorks.title: Use it for membership and failure detection
howItWorks.text: Each node keeps a heartbeat counter that it increments and gossips. If a node's counter has not increased for a while in anyone's table, it is suspected to be down, and that opinion spreads too. SWIM-style protocols add direct and indirect probes to cut false alarms.

howItWorks.title: It is eventually consistent by design
howItWorks.text: At any moment different nodes hold slightly different views. That is acceptable for membership, load figures and configuration hints. It is not a substitute for consensus when nodes must agree on a single value or order.

pros: Scales to thousands of nodes with constant work per node
No single point of failure, and robust to lost messages and crashed nodes
Simple to implement and reason about
Self-healing: missed updates are repaired on later rounds
cons: Redundant messages: the same news is received many times
Convergence time grows slowly with size (log N rounds) and depends on the interval
Cannot give strong guarantees such as a single agreed order
whenToUse: Cluster membership and failure detection (Cassandra, Consul, Serf)
Spreading configuration, load statistics and routing hints
Anti-entropy: reconciling replicas in the background
whenNotToUse: Decisions that need agreement (who is the leader, did this commit): use consensus
Small clusters where a simple broadcast or a coordinator is easier
pitfalls: A gossip interval so short that it floods the network, or so long that failures are noticed minutes late
Setting failure suspicion too aggressively, so slow nodes are declared dead
Relying on gossip alone for correctness of data
Ignoring network partitions, where each side converges on a different view
